summary: Describes the IANA considerations for PPP over Ethernet (PPPoE), meaning how code points for the protocol are assigned. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Messages use code numbers for different meanings. This note says how new numbers get handed out so none are reused.

subtitle: Who may claim a PPPoE TAG value or Code field, and which ones were already taken.

tldr.problem: PPP over Ethernet (PPPoE) has two name spaces, the TAG and the Code field, and without a registry two vendors could use the same value for different things.
tldr.mechanism: IANA sets up one registry for 16-bit TAG values and one for 8-bit Code fields, both handed out First Come First Served, and this RFC lists the values already in use as reserved.
tldr.outcome: Anyone who wants a new TAG or Code must give a name, a description and a point of contact, which helps stop the same value meaning different functions.

today: RFC 4937 is an Informational RFC and has not been obsoleted or updated. It records the PPPoE TAG and Code registries as they were set up in June 2007.

sections.title: Why PPPoE Needs Registries
sections.content:
This document gives guidance to the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA) about registering values for the PPP over Ethernet protocol (PPPoE), which is defined in RFC 2516. It follows the rules for IANA considerations sections in BCP 26 (RFC 2434).

It also reserves the PPPoE TAG values and PPPoE packet Code fields that are, or have been, in use on the Internet. RFC 2516 defines two name spaces that need registration: the PPPoE TAG and the PPPoE Code field.
sections.eli5: PPPoE uses numbers to say what a message part means. Someone has to keep a list so two people do not use the same number for different jobs.

sections.title: Registration Policy for TAG Values
sections.content:
IANA has set up a registry of PPPoE TAG Values. These are 16-bit values. The values already in use are reserved by this document. Every other value between 0 and 65535 is assigned by IANA under the First Come First Served policy from RFC 2434.

Anyone asking for an assignment MUST provide a TAG-Name, a description of the usage and a point of contact. A document reference SHOULD also be provided.
sections.eli5: If you want a new TAG number, you ask, say what it is for and who to contact. The first person to ask gets it.

sections.title: Reserved TAG Values
sections.content:
The reserved list covers the TAGs from RFC 2516 (for example Service-Name at 0x0101, AC-Name at 0x0102 and Host-Uniq at 0x0103), the three credit and metrics TAGs from RFC 4938 (0x0106 to 0x0108), and PPP-Max-Payload (0x0120) from RFC 4638.

Four more come from a Work in Progress by Carrel and others, listed as [CARREL]: HURL, MOTM, IP_Route_Add. The three error TAGs, Service-Name-Error, AC-System-Error and Generic-Error, sit at 0x0201 to 0x0203.
sections.eli5: Some numbers are already used, so they are written down as taken. The table shows which number means what.

sections.title: Code Fields and Their Reserved Values
sections.content:
IANA also keeps a registry of PPPoE Active Discovery Code fields. These are 8-bit values. Codes already in use are reserved, and all other values between 0 and 255 are assigned First Come First Served. A packet name, a usage description and a point of contact MUST be supplied, and a document reference SHOULD be.

The reserved codes include PADI (9), PADO (7), PADR (25), PADS (101) and PADT (167) from RFC 2516, plus PADG, PADC and PADQ (10 to 12) from RFC 4938, and PADM and PADN (211 and 212) from [CARREL]. Code 0 is the PPP Session Stage.
sections.eli5: Message types get numbers too, and the same rule applies: ask first, and some numbers are already taken for well-known messages.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC says it focuses on IANA considerations. As such, it should help remove the possibility of the same PPPoE Code field or PPPoE TAG value being used for different functionalities. It adds no other security discussion.
sections.eli5: Keeping one clear list means nobody mixes up two different things that share a number.
